Auteurs : R. Ayed, A. Ben Brik. Cible : conférence IEEE – shortlistBigData / ICMLA / SSCI / FUZZ-IEEE(a arbitrer). Problématique. Détection non supervisée des transactionsfrauduleuses ou anormales dans le cadre du paiement par cartes prépayées en Tunisie. Le travail s’appuie sur les données réelles de Pluxee (transactions de mars et avril,∼380 MB de CSV bruts, partitionnees par mois et par sous-fichier). Approche. Pipeline reproductible articulé autour de clustering K-means + analyse comporte- mentale + agrégation par commerçant / ville / gouvernorat tunisien. Refactoring du notebook d’exploration en modules Python testables, avecconfigs YAML par modele etMakefile de repro- duction. Critique interne formalisee (CRITIQUE.md + PLAN_REVISION.md, 15 jours-homme). Contributions attendues. — Cartographie des comportements de paiement en contexte tunisien (1ere étude publiée a notre connaissance) — Pipeline de detection d’anomalies sur cartes prépayées (cas d’usage operationnel pour les acteurs financiers tunisiens) — Code et configurat

— Cartographie des comportements de paiement en contexte tunisien (1ere étude publiée a notre connaissance) — Pipeline de detection d’anomalies sur cartes prépayées (cas d’usage operationnel pour les acteurs financiers tunisiens) — Code et configurations reproductibles 1.3.2 Axe 2 – Reproducibility-First Multi-Component Forecasting on BVMT Titre : Reproducibility-First Multi-Component Forecasting for Illiquid Equity Markets : Base- lines, Ablations, and a Documented Discrepancy on the Tunisian Stock Exchange. Auteurs : A. Ben Brik, A.A. Fraj. Cible : conférence IEEE – shortlist préparée (ieee_conferences_shortlist). Problématique. L’IA financière est massivement conçue pour les marchés liquides développés. Elle se brise sur les marchés émergentsthin liquidity: gaps de continuité, hétérogénéité des échelles par titre, pas de derives, presse multilingue (francais + arabe sur la BVMT), absence de benchmarks publics. LaBourse des Valeurs Mobilières de Tunis (BVMT)– 68 titres, volume 0.5–2 MDT / jour – est un cas d’étude representatif. A notre connaissance,aucun systeme de deep learning n’a ete publiesur les actions BVMT (recherche IEEE Xplore / ACM / arXiv / SSRN / Google Scholar, janvier 2026). 5/278

Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 1.3.3 Axe 3 – Orchestrated N-Agent Centipede Game for Cooperative AI Titre : An Orchestrated N-Agent Centipede Game Framework for Cooperative Artificial Intelligence Systems. Auteur : A. Ben Brik(auteur unique). Statut : en cours de revisionavant resoumission. Problématique. La cooperation est un défi central des systèmes IA multi-agents. LeCentipede Game (Rosenthal, 1981) formalise la tensionbenefice court-terme individuelvs performance long- terme collective, mais il est restreint a deux joueurs. Or les architectures cooperatives modernes (tutorat intelligent, robotique collaborative, RL multi-agents) impliquent generalementN agents + un orchestrateur central. Approche. Extension du Centipede Game classique vers un cadrea N agents avec orchestra- teur, capable de : — modeliser des stratégies cooperatives au-dela du contexte dyadique — etudier l’influence du contrôleur central sur les decisions individuelles (retardement de la defection précoce) — ameliorer les résultats collectifs en environnements stratégiques Lien avec les autres axes.Ce cadre fournit unbenchmark game-théoriquepour evaluer les agents pédagogiques LLM de l’Axe 4(Educational Centipede Game). Il prolonge egalement l’orchestration multi-agents deployee dansESB-Learning (cf. §2.3) etRecruScore (cf. §2.2). 1.3.4 Axe 4 – Mean Field RL for LLM-Based Pedagogical Agents Titre : Mean Field Reinforcement Learning for LLM-Based Pedagogical Agents in Higher Education (proposal de recherche structurant). eur : A. Ben Brik. Statut : axe de recherche en cours de formalisation, proposal de these / programme doctoral. Problématique. Les systèmes éducatifs a base de LLM sont aujourd’hui majoritairement1-to-1 (un tuteur IA pour un etudiant) ou bases sur des règles fixes. Ils ne modélisent pas explicitement la dynamique collective d’une cohorte, alors même que l’enseignement supérieur (notre cas d’usage ESB) implique des grandes classes, des publics hétérogènes, des ressources limitées et des objectifs pédagogiques multiples. Approche – combinaison originale. — LLM-based Agentic AI– agents specialises (tuteur, evaluation, modeling etudiant, curri- culum, peer grouping, safety, teacher assistant) — Mean Field Games(Lasry & Lions, 2007) – representation de la cohorte etudiante comme une distribution de populationmt(x) = 1 N ∑ iδxi(t) — Mean Field Reinforcement Learning– politiqueπθ(at|xi(t),mt) qui conditionne l’action pedagogique sur l’etat individuelET sur l’etat collectif — Educational Centipede Game– benchmark game-théorique original (extension de l’axe 3) mesurant la cooperation, laproductive struggle, l’over-helping, et la confiance long-terme entre etudiants et tuteur IA 7/278

Auteurs : A. Ben Brik, Ichraf [...], Sana [...]. Statut : manuscrit finalisé – en attente de l’étude empiriquepour soumission. Continuité avec le premier article.Le premier article co-écrit avecIchraf et Sana a posé le modèle qualitatif du Sustainability Expectation–Perception Gapet identifié une divergence systématique entre les perceptions des parties prenantes universitaires et leurs attentes en matière de durabilité.Le présent article (deuxième de la série)opérationnalise ce modèle au moyen d’une enquête quantitative auprès des parties pr

divergence systématique entre les perceptions des parties prenantes universitaires et leurs attentes en matière de durabilité.Le présent article (deuxième de la série)opérationnalise ce modèle au moyen d’une enquête quantitative auprès des parties prenantes internes. Problématique. La légitimité méthodologique des indices composites de durabilité dépend de façon critique duschéma de pondérationadopté. Trois familles dominent la littérature – techniques empiriques (Structural Equation Modeling – SEM), méthodes multicritères normatives (Analytic Hierarchy Process – AHP) et approches data-driven d’optimisation par IA – mais aucune ne réconcilie pleinement validité théorique, interprétabilité par les parties prenantes et robustesse adaptative. Approche – cadre hybride multi-paradigme.Le papier propose unframework de pondé- ration hybrideintégrant : — Poids empiriquesdérivés de la structure latente viaSEM (modèle de Gap structurel : Expectation–Perception Gap). — Poids normatifspilotés par les experts viaAHP. — Poids adaptatifsoptimisés par des algorithmes d’apprentissage IA. — Méta-architecture agrégeant les trois vecteurs de poids avec calibration stratégique des contributions épistémiques. — Analyse de sensibilitédes méta-poids +simulation Monte Carlopour la robustesse sous incertitude. 8/278

La tarification actuarielle d’uneflotte automobile(parc de véhicules détenus par une entreprise ou une collectivité) constitue un cas d’usage central en assurance non-vie : faut-il appliquer à chaque flotte laprime moyenne du portefeuille collectif (statistiquement robuste mais insensible à l’expérience propre de l’assuré) ou laprime calculée sur sa seule sinistralité historique(sensible mais statistiquement instable, surtout pour les petites flottes)? Lathéorie de la crédibilité(Bühlmann, 1967; Bühlmann & Straub, 1970; Jewell, 1975) propose un cadrebayésien empiriquerésolvant ce dilemme par une combinaison convexe : ˆPflotte = Z·¯Xflotte + (1−Z)·µcollectif où lefacteur de crédibilitéZ∈[0, 1] est une fonction croissante duvolume d’exposition au risque de la flotte et décroissante durapport variance inter-groupes / variance intra-groupe. Le modèle est étendu à une structureBühlmann-Straub pour intégrer uneexposition variable(durée et nombre de véhicules par période), puis enrichi par desniveaux hiérarchiques(segments de flottes – VL, VUL, PL, deux-roues – ou secteurs d’activité de l’assuré). Verrous traités par les deux mémoires. — Hétérogénéité intra-flotte: composition variable d’une flotte (mix carrosseries, usages, kilométrages, zones de circulation), exigeant unemodélisation à exposition au

es – ou secteurs d’activité de l’assuré). Verrous traités par les deux mémoires. — Hétérogénéité intra-flotte: composition variable d’une flotte (mix carrosseries, usages, kilométrages, zones de circulation), exigeant unemodélisation à exposition au risque variable. — Effet de structure et taille de flotte: forte asymétrie du portefeuille entre micro-flottes (< 10 véhicules) et grands comptes (> 1000 véhicules), qui impose uncalibrage différencié du facteur de crédibilité. — Estimation des composantes de variance: choix entre estimateurs non-paramétriques (méthode des moments) et estimateurs maximum de vraisemblance dans le cadre desmodèles linéaires mixtes, comparaison empirique sur le portefeuille Covéa. — Validation prédictive: évaluation hors-échantillon de laprime de crédibilité vs prime collective vs prime individuelle (erreur quadratique pondérée par exposition, lift, écart-type des résidus), backtesting sur cohortes glissantes. Données réelles – Covéa.Les deux mémoires exploitent desdonnées réelles fournies par le groupe Covéa(un des premiers assureurs français, regroupant les marques MAAF, MMA et GMF) : historique de sinistralité du portefeuilleflottes automobiles, expositions au risque (véhicules- année), caractéristiques techniques (type, puissance, usage, zone géographique), ainsi que lesprimes d’assurancede référence. Cet accès à un jeu de données de marché représentatif confère aux travaux une portée empiriquedépassant le seul cadre académique et permet lavalidation industrielle des modèles proposés. Evaluation of Large Language Models in Simulating Real-world Engineering Scenarios and Decision Making: A Comparative Study of ChatGPT-4o, Gemini, and Perplexity Abstract. Integrating real-world simulations and decision-making scenarios through case studies has been shown to enhance students’ critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Prior research highlighted a gap in faculty ca pacity to create or access such materials, an issue particularly acute in developing c oun- tries. This study explores the potential of three prominent LLMs, namely ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.0, and Perplexity, to generate high-quality case studies for graduate engineering education. Our evaluation employs a mu lti-layered methodology combining: (1) a linguistic analysis using standard NLP metri cs; (2) automated mixed-method assessments using four LLMs; and (3) mixed- method evaluation by three Subject Matter Experts (SMEs). Our findings re - vealed that while Perplexity produced the most readable content, it fail ed along with Gemini to meet the minimum required word count. The SMEs unanimous- ly ranked ChatGPT-4o as superior across all performance dimensions. This study shed light on several LLM limitations, such as limited narrative flow, lack of depth, compelling storytelling and academic rigor, failure to meet explicit in- structional requirements, and instances of fake or inaccurate citations. The se challenges reinforce the necessity for a “human -in-the-loop" approach. Our study offers a balanced and evidence-based perspective on the r ole of LLMs in augmenting, rather than replacing, human expertise in case study development. Keywords: Emerging Technologies, Applied Computing, Computer-managed Instruction, Experiential Learning, Large Language Models, Generative AI, NLP, Natural Language Processing, Case Studies, Engineering Education, De- cision-making, Critical Thinking. 1 Introduction Exposing students to experiential learning opportunities has been recognized as a cornerstone pedagogical approach to bridge the gap between theoretical kno wledge and practical, hands-on problem-solving, which is particularly vital in the con text of engineering education [1]. Experiential learning is a hands-on approach th at exposes students to real-world experiences through active participation and reflective th inking on experience. This approach has been proven to facilitate deeper understan ding of the subject matter [2], stimulate critical thinking and problem-solving [3], foster adaptability competencies [1], boost students' intrinsic motivation [4] and enhan ce employability [5]. Experiential learning can take many forms such as laboratory work, internships, field trips, capstone and integrated projects, community service activities, workshops, simulations, and role playing. 56/278

Such an exposure can potentially allow students to practice decision-making and develop critical thinking and pro blem- solving skills while considering the broader context pertaining to ethics and sus taina- ble development [7]. Although case studies hold significant potential, engineering faculty are not gener - ally well positioned to seize these opportunities for many reasons: • Engineering graduates are recruited and rewarded for solving problems, s o they should be trained on how to solve workplace problems. However, engineerin g problems are inherently complex, ill-defined, and multi-disciplinary [8]. This makes it difficult for faculty to propose authentic case studies that simultaneousl y replicate real-world scenarios and at the same meet specific learning outcomes without making oversimplifying assumptions [9]. • Engineering faculty might not have any professional experience or access to up-to- date engineering trends and solutions [10-11]. This makes it challenging for them to develop authentic case studies that reflect current industry practices. • Creating meaningful and up to date case studies is a resource-intensive endeavo r for faculty members [12]. Heavy workload, limited time and resources, lack of Problem Based Learning (PBL) training and the over-focus of faculty promo tion policies on research productivity at the expense of pedagogical innovation amplify the opportunity cost for faculty to invest in developing authentic case studies [12]. • Although there are som

The study spanned from 10 January 2025 to 20 March 2025. Our research methodology unfolds in three distinct stages: case study generation, automated LLM-based evaluation, and expert assessment. We contextualized our study within the setting of the graduate course “Managing Big Data Projects”. This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive under - standing of the technical and managerial aspects of managing big data projects, while raising awareness of the broader ethical and legal implications. CLO2: Develop and demonstrate advanced project management skills specifi cally tailored for big data projects. CLO3: Apply principles of data governance and ethics in the context of big data projects. CLO4: Apply analytical and critical thinking skills to solve complex prob lems pertaining to managing big data projects. In fact, the LLMs tended to restructure or rewrite the case study as opposed to incrementally refining prior outputs. These limitations are attributed to the fact that unlike human s, LLMs lack persistent memory across sessions and interactions. LLMs primarily rel y on regressive language modeling, leveraging probabilistic predictions to gene rate future words and sentences based on learned patterns from extensive training data , rather than strictly adhering to predefined formatting or instructional constraints [ 38]. Moreover, like most transformer-based architectures, these models are constrained by finite context windows, which limit the amount of text they can process in a single query and hence their ability to maintain dialogue coherence over longer interactions. For instance, ChatGPT-4o supports a maximum context window of 8,192 tokens per query, Perplexity (Free Tier) is limited to 4,000 tokens, while Gemini 2.0 Flash ex - tends this capacity to 1 M tokens, encompassing both input text and generated re- sponses. When these context thresholds are exceeded, the models truncate earlier segments of the conversation to accommodate new inputs and outputs. Our research showed that LLM-generated case studies require thorough human oversight, including rigorous fact-checking, stylistic refinement, and narrative en- hancement, before being integrated into educational settings. Our research contributes to the growing body of evidence on the transformative po- tential of LLMs in equipping future engineers with the skills needed to address com- plex, interdisciplinary, and ethically nuanced engineering challenges and experiential learning experiences. This study has many limitations. For instance, it has a narrow scope, restricted to a single course context, three prominent LLM architectures, and a limited pool of three SMEs. Future research should aim to broaden this scope by incorporating additio nal LLMs such as Copilot, DeepSeek, and Grok, while also engaging a more diverse and extensive panel of assessors. We also call on AI developers and technology providers to enhance their mod els’ context awareness, reliability, and responsiveness to specific instructional require- ments, especially in the context of rigorous academic settings. While LLMs are not yet ready to independently generate publishable or classroom- ready case studies, they hold tremendous promise as co-creative collaborators. With proper frameworks, human oversight, and ethical and responsible usage, L LMs are poised to become beacons of hope for educators in developing countr ies, enabling the cost-effective access to high-quality, locally contextualized case studies and democr a- tizing access to innovative pedagogical teaching instruments. However, earlier research has identified a prevailing gap in assessment competency amon g faculty. Rooted in established interdisciplinary concepts and theories, this study ai ms to explore the usage of ChatGPT-4 as a co-pilot to guide faculty in assessment design refinement. To achieve this goal, we adopt a conversational analysis approach, contextualizing our study within the settings of the final exam of the senior course “Wireless Sensor Networks”, offered at ESPRIT School of Engineering. We propose a framework to guide the implementation of the conversational analysis method. Our research results illustrate the merits, potentials, and limitations of using ChatGPT as a co-pilot to assist faculty in refining the assessment design process. It also brings into evidence the importance of keeping a ‘human in the loop’ perspective during the faculty-ChatGPT assessment co-creation activities. Our study can pave the way for further research on other potential applications of “Human -AI co-creation” and augmented man-machine intelligence in a CDIO engineering education. INTRODUCTION Assessing the extent to which engineering students achieve their program learning outcomes upon graduation is of paramount importance for educational effectiveness , continuous improvement and for meeting accreditation requirements (Ali, 2023) . Program Learning Outcomes (PLOs) are generally expressed as broad statements that capture the cumulative disciplinary knowledge, skills, and abilities that engineering students should demonstrate upon completing their educational program. For assessment, PLOs are often mapped to indivi dual courses within the program and the PLOs-Courses mapping matrix showcases how individual courses, collectively, contribute towards achieving the overarching goals set by the program learning outcomes. Unlike the broader PLOs, Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) are specific to individual classes, focusing on personal and interpersonal skills , knowledge areas, and product, process, system, and service building skills (CDIO, 2020) that students are expected 82/278

The design of effective learning assessment instruments to probe students’ achievement of course learning outcomes is among the key pillars of effective engineering progra ms, as reflected for instance by CDIO standard 11 (CDIO, 2020). Effective course learning assessment goes beyond evaluating students' competencies and grading their academic performance. Its primary added value lies in guiding instruc tors to continuously refine their teaching material and methods, thus providing a 360-degree loo p of critical feedback to continuously improve students’ learning and faculty teaching. For example, if an assessment shows that students are struggling with a specific learning outcome, it incites the instructor to revisit the related teaching material and approaches, providing a potentially better learning opportunity for the next cohort. Despite the importance of designing effective learning assessments in engineering education, earlier research (e.g. Palm, 2019; Villarroel et al., 2018; Fook & Sidhu, 2010) revealed that not all faculty members possess the required competencies in designing authentic learning assessments that are aligned with the stated course objectives and learning outcomes. While the challenges of designing authentic assessments that are valid, reliable, and enga ging are well documented (Heritage, 2022), some faculty are still struggling with developing appropriate assessment instructions and establishing clear

tcomes. While the challenges of designing authentic assessments that are valid, reliable, and enga ging are well documented (Heritage, 2022), some faculty are still struggling with developing appropriate assessment instructions and establishing clear scoring rubrics. In fact, while some faculty may demonstrate superior performance as subject matter experts, they sometimes lack the necessary knowledge and skills to effectively design authentic assessments. Guskey (20 15) argued that faculty professional development programs often privileged teaching methods and technology integration over assessment practices. In its coverage of the actions needed to enhance faculty teaching competence, CDIO standard 10 (CDIO, 2020) emph asizes “assessment of student learning” as an integral teaching competence and highlights the need for faculty development in this area. For the past years, there has been a growing interest in the application of Generative AI (GAI) and AI-driven conversational models to enhance students’ learning and faculty teaching. Previous research has suggested that AI chatbots can effectively assist faculty in creating exam questions and grading students' responses (see, for example, Cheung et al., 2023; Daun & Brings, 2023; Grévisse, 2023; Skrabut, 2023, Chapter 4). However, these s tudies have mainly focused on showcasing how intelligent natural language processing tools can assist faculty in proposing practice exercises and a variety of assessments, including interactive quizzes, multiple choice exam questions, and fill-in-the-blank test questions. Such an approach tends to favor the passive consumption of information among faculty, without enhancing their creativity and critical thinking skills in designing effective assessment instruments. It emphasizes the role of talk- in-interaction and how conversational turns are constructed among participants to achieve mutual unde rstanding (Sidnell & Stivers, 2013). Second, it recognizes that when ChatGPT deviates from the context of the assigned task, human intervention is needed to guide it back on track, ensuring relevance of the response. Third, our feedback can help ChatGPT to continuously improve its training model and hence enhance its reliability. Our research findings provide evidence on the merits of the collaboration between humans and AI in co-creation and new idea generations, as suggested by the AuI and co-creati on frameworks (Dellermann et al., 2021; Xue et al., 2022). Our research a lso illustrates how knowledge can be constructed during the exam co-design collaboration with ChatGPT through active engagement, iterative interactions, and feedback. This process aligns with the principles of constructivism (Jonassen, 1999). As mentioned by Kamoun et al. (2023), these meaningful engagements between the human and the AI-driven conversational model are most likely to become life-long learni ng competencies for faculty. CONCLUSION AND SUGGESTIONS FOR FUTURE RESEARCH This study was motivated by earlier research findings that highlighted the prevaili ng gap in assessment competency among faculty and the need for creative and effective solutions to address this shortcoming. It adopted a conversational analysis approach, within the context of a senior engineering course’s final exam, to showcase the potentials and limitations of using ChatGPT-4 as a co-pilot in assisting faculty to refine the assessment desig

hortcoming. It adopted a conversational analysis approach, within the context of a senior engineering course’s final exam, to showcase the potentials and limitations of using ChatGPT-4 as a co-pilot in assisting faculty to refine the assessment design process. Unlike most related previous studies that promoted the passive consumption of information among faculty by simply soliciting ChatGPT to propose assessment questions, our approach promotes collaboration and co-creation. It uses ChatGPT as a co-pilot for assessment design refinement, while keeping a ‘human in the loop’ perspective. Our research contributes to advancing the body of knowledge in engineering education by providing evidence that, when properly orchestrated, active engagement and meaningful interactive conversations with GAI systems can actively promote higher-order thinking skills among faculty, enabling them to collaborate with GAI chatbots to co-create assessment tasks that reflect better creativity and enhanced effectiveness. This can pave t he way for further research on other potenti al applications of “Human -AI co- creation” and augmented man - machine intelligence in a CDIO engineering education. This study has several limitations: First it is of limited scope, being focused on a single course, which also makes the results not necessarily generalizable to other educational context s. Second, being focused exclusively on the final exam, our study does not consider other forms of assessment instruments such as projects . Third, our study does not incorporate student feedback or perspectives on the outcomes of the co-created assessment. Research is underway to address some of the limitations mentioned above. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 A Hybrid Multi-Paradigm Weighting Framework for Composite Sustainability Indices: Integrating Structural Equation Modeling, Analytic Hierarchy Process, and AI-Based Optimization Author Name Abstract Composite sustainability indices are widely used to synthesize multidimensional per- formance into actionable decision-support tools. However, the methodological legitimacy of such indices remains critically dependent on the weighting scheme adopted. Existing approaches typically rely on either empirical techniques (e.g., Structural Equation Model- ing), normative multi-criteria decision-making methods (e.g., Analytic Hierarchy Process), or data-driven optimization frameworks rooted in artiﬁcial intelligence. Each paradigm embod- ies distinct epistemological assumptions, yet no single approach fully reconciles theoretical validity, stakeholder interpretability, and adaptive robustness. RecruScore: An Agent-Based AI Ecosystem for Enhancing Employability and Lifelong Learning in Higher Education Aymen Ben Brik Heni Abidi aymen.benbrik@esprit.tn heni.abidi@esprit.tn AI-enabled recruitment support, explainable matching, and li felong learning ESPRIT School of Engineering - ESPRIT School of Business Higher education needs stronger links between curricula, employability, and lifelong learning. Support for CV writing, job targeting, interview preparation, and training is often fragmented. Students and alumni struggle to translate academic achievements into job-ready, offer-specific profiles. Recruiters and universities also lack scalable, transparent tools for readiness assessment and screening. This initiative uses responsible AI to align academic learning with labor-market needs by creating feedback loops from job offers, alumni paths, and skill gaps, while improving application quality, interview readiness, and access to targeted upskilling for students and alumni. Data collection → CV analysis → Hybrid matching → Agentic interview → Feedback & learning Continuous loop: CV improvement, matching, mock interviews, and training recommendations. Turns recruitment preparation into a learning journey: CV enhancement, job targeting, interview practice, and course recommendations are connected in one student-facing workflow. Goes beyond isolated job boards or ATS tools by connecting candidates, recruiters, administrators, and trainers in a continuous feedback loop grounded in curricula and human oversight. nd development of SmartNutriTrack, an innovative intelligent nutrition application that combines computer vision-based food recognition and personalized meal planning. The project addresses limitations of existing applications by automating food tracking through CNN models (VGG16 and MobileNetV2) and generating adaptive nutrition plans using a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system with Llama 3.1. The microservices architecture, developed with React.js, Node.js/Express and Python/FastAPI, enables seamless integration of AI components. The hybrid methodology combines CRISP-DM for AI model development and Scrum for the software development cycle. Results demonstrate 87% accuracy in visual recognition, 40% improvement in protein targets achievement, and 70% reduction in user input time. SmartNutriTrack represents a significant advancement in digital nutrition applications, providing a comprehensive and scientifically-grounded solution for personalized nutrition tracking and planning. Livrable 1 – Production RDI A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 BGA Accreditation – ABB Activities A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 5. PLAR – Program Learning Assessment Review Definition. The PLAR (Program Learning Assessment Review) is the programme-level quality auditrequired by BGA. It aggregates the CARs of the constituent courses (§ 4) along the Introduced/Reinforced/ Emphasized (I/R/E) trajectory in order to evaluate thedegree of attainment of each Program Learning Outcome (PLO)and to drive continuous improvement at programme level. Methodology – 5-section PLAR template Reporting structure (one document per PLO trajectory).Each PLAR follows a five-section template, harmonised across the three IMA programmes audited (BA, LBC-BI, LBC-BIS) : 1. Section 1 – Program Learning Outcomes– table of the programme’s PLOs, withCom- mon/Specifictyping (Common PLOs are SDG-aligned and shared across IMA programmes; Specific PLOs are unique to the programme). 2. Section 2 – Methodology– selection of the PLOs to assess (typically≥2 per programme : one Common, SDG-alignedand oneSpecific), and selection of the contributing courses along the I/R/E trajectory. 3. Section 3 – Benchmark Indicator (MBI)– theMinimum Benchmark Indicatoris set at 60% : a PLO is considered achieved when the percentage of students scoring≥60% on the related CLOs reaches the threshold. 4. Section 4 – Results– per-CLO performance, per-course consolidation, per-PLO aggregation, and overall verdict (goal met / not met). 5. Section 5 – Recommendations for Continuous Improvement– corrective actions feeding back into syllabi, course scheduling, assessment design and faculty training. Selection rule (CLOs→PLOs). For each course mapped to a selected PLO, the CLOs already linked to the PLO via the alignment matrix (§ 2)

rovement– corrective actions feeding back into syllabi, course scheduling, assessment design and faculty training. Selection rule (CLOs→PLOs). For each course mapped to a selected PLO, the CLOs already linked to the PLO via the alignment matrix (§ 2) are extracted, and the percentage of students reaching the 60% benchmark on each of these CLOs is computed. ThePLO attainment ratefor the course is the mean of its PLO-related CLOs; theprogramme-level PLO attainmentis the mean across courses along the I/R/E trajectory. Indicators computed for each PLAR. — Attainment rate per PLO(% of students reaching the 60% benchmark, aggregated across the I/R/E trajectory). — Pedagogical coverage of each PLO(number of contributing courses, distribution across I/R/E levels and semesters). — CLO-to-PLO traceability(per-CLO performance feeding back into the PLO score). — CAR→PLAR consistency (alignment between module-level CAR observations and programme-level PLO profile). — Action planfor the next cohort (curriculum revision, course scheduling, assessment design, faculty training). Tooling and frequency. — Data sources: CAR results (§ 4), CLO→PLO alignment matrix (§ 2), grade extracts from Tekouin/ESB IS. — Consolidation : master spreadsheetPLOs Assessment (IMA).ods (one row per course, one column per CLO, weighted aggregation per PLO). 23/49 192/278

Livrable 1 – Production RDI A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 International Journal of Quality and Service Sciences What Makes a University Sustainable in the Eyes of its Core Community? Sustainability Expectation–Perception Gap Purpose –This study adopts a behavioural, stakeholder centred approach to identify the key dimensions of university sustainability valued by internal stakeholders (students, faculty members and administrative staff). It examines how they prioritize environmental, social, and economic dimensions, assesses gaps between expectations and perceived initiatives, and proposes a composite score to support the University Sustainability Performance Index (USPI). Design/methodology/approach – This study uses a qualitative case study approach within a single university, conducting semi -structured interviews with internal stakeholders to explore perceptions of environmental, social, and economic sustainability. Thematic analysis identified sustainability university dimensions. Findings – The results reveal gaps between stakeholder perceptions and expectations. Socially, student well -being and community engag ement need stronger structuring. Environmental initiatives are recognized, yet sustainable mobility and awareness require better formalization. Economic gaps remain significant, especially in energy optimization, financial governance and sustainable investment. Research limitations – The study focuses on internal stakeholders in a specific context. Future research could include external stakeholders and cross-institutional comparisons. Practical implications – The USPI provides university leaders with a transparent, stakeholder- driven decision-support tool to assess sustainability performance and prioritize strategic actions effectively. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 International Journal of Quality and Service Sciences Introduction Sustainability in higher education institutions (HEIs) has become a strategic and societal imperative in response to growing environmental, social, economic, and governance challenges worldwide (Velazquez et al., 2006; Alshuwaikhat & Abubakar, 2008). Universities are no longer perceived solely as knowledge-producing entities; they are increasingly expected to act as transformative agents capable of shaping sustainable development trajectories (Popowska & Sady, 2024; Sugiarto et al., 2022). In alignment with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), sustainability in HEIs extends beyond environmental stewardship to encompass social equity, economic viability, institutional governance, and academic excellence (Alshuwaikhat et al., 2016). Despite the proliferation of sustainability rankings, reporting frameworks, and performance indicators, existing assessment tools often remain predominantly operational and managerial in nature (Sonetti et al., 2016; Horan & O’Regan, 2021). They typically rely on externally defined metrics and institutional reporting mechanisms, while giving limited attention to how sustainability is perceived and pri oritized by the university’s own academic community. This represents a significant conceptual gap. Sustainability is not merely a technical or administrative construct; it is also a socially constructed and behaviourally interpreted phenomenon shaped by stakeholder perceptions, expectations, and value systems (Dagiliūtė et al., 2018; Zhao & Zou, 2023). Stakeholder theory (Freeman, 1984) posits that organizational sustainability depends on the integration of diverse stakeholder interests. Within HEIs, intern al stakeholders, particularly students and faculty, play a central role in shaping the institution’s sustainability identity (Alshuwaikhat & Abubakar, 2008; Disterheft et al., 2013). Students seek meaningful education, employability, and ethical alignment with societal challenges, while faculty members emphasize academic integrity, research impact, and institutional mission. Yet, little empirical research has systematically examined how these core actors interpret sustainability, how they prioritize its dim ensions, and how they evaluate institutional performance relative to their expectations (Dagiliūtė et al., 2018; Yasin et al., 2024). Addressing this gap is essential for developing assessment tools that genuinely reflect institutional realities rather than externally imposed benchmarks. If sustainability indices are to guide strategic decision -making effectively, they must be grounded in stakeholder -defined priorities (Velazquez et al., 2006; Alshuwaikhat et al., 2016). In this context, understanding what makes a university “sustainable” in the eyes of its core community becomes a critical research question. This study adopts a behavioural and stakeholder centred perspective to analyse the sustainability preferences of students, faculty members, and administrative staff within a case- study university. Through qualitative inquiry, it explores how these actors interpret environmental, social, and economic sustainability dimensions, how they hierarchize them, and how they perceive institutional performance. Literature review Stakeholder Theory and University Sustainability Stakeholder theory provides a foundational lens for understanding sustainability in higher education institutions (HEIs). Originally developed in strategic management (Freeman, 1984), the theory argues that organizational legitimacy and long -term performance depend on the ability to recognize, balance, and integrate the interests of multiple stakeholder groups rather than privileging a single dom inant constituency. Organizations are embedded in networks of relationships, and value is generated through ongoing interactions among actors with diverse expectations. Mitchell et al., (1997) introduced the stakeholder salience framework, emphasizing that stakeholders differ in terms of power, legitimacy, and urgency. Within HEIs, a wide range of stakeholders coexist, including students, faculty members, administrative staff, employers, accreditation bodies, local communities, and policymakers. However, in ternal stakeholders, particularly students and faculty, occupy a structurally central position. They are not only recipients of sustainability policies but active agents who interpret, enact, and sometimes contest institutional sustainability agendas. More recent developments in stakeholder theory emphasize relationality and value co-creation (Freeman et al., 2010). From this perspective, sustainability is not merely implemented through top-down governance mechanisms or infrastructure investments; it emerge s from shared meaning-making processes and collective engagement. Universities can thus be understood as ecosystems in which sustainability outcomes are co -produced through interactions between institutional strategies and stakeholder perceptions. While st akeholder theory provides a strong normative and relational foundation for understanding sustainability in higher education, the empirical literature on campus sustainability has developed along several thematic trajectories. Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) are increasingly recognized as pivotal actors in fostering sustainable development and addressing global environmental challenges. Often described as "small cities" due to their significant populations and complex operations (Alshuwaikhat & Abubakar, 2008; Velazquez et al., 2006; Min -Allah & Alrashed, 2020; Murshed, 2020), universities wield substantial direct and indirect impacts on the environment through their energy consumption, material use, waste generation, and daily activities. Consequently, the concept of a "green campus" has emerged as a comprehensive approach to integrating sustainability principles across physical infrastructure, academic curricula, research, and institutional governance (Disterheft et al., 2013; Sugiarto et al., 2022). Conceptualization, Frameworks, and Assessment Tools for Green Campuses A significant portion of the lit erature focuses on defining, conceptualizing, and assessing sustainability within HEIs. Early work proposed comprehensive managerial models for a "sustainable university" (Velazquez et al., 2006) and integrated approaches to campus sustainability (Alshuwai khat & Abubakar, 2008). The evolving nature of "campus sustainability" is often understood in a broad sense, encompassing physical, educational, and institutional dimensions (Disterheft et al., 2013). Researchers note a shift from simplistic "going green" trends to a more holistic, systemic understanding that integrates environmental, social, and economic dimensions (Alshuwaikhat et al., 2016; Sugiarto et al., 2022; Popowska & Sady, 2024). The development and application of assessment tools and ranking syst ems are central to measuring progress and benchmarking sustainability efforts. Prominent examples include the UI GreenMetric World University Rankings (Fatah & Waro, 2025) and the Sustainability Tracking, Assessment & Rating System (STARS) (Urbanski & Leal, 2015; Zhu & Dewancker, 2021; Washington-Ottombre, 2024). Other frameworks like AISHE (Auditing Instrument for Sustainability in Higher Education) (Lambrechts & Ceulemans, 2013) and SAQ (Sustainability Assessment Questionnaire) (Alshuwaikhat et al., 2016) are also utilized. Context and Objectives Context Sustainability in higher education institutions (HEIs) has emerged as a critical global priority, driven by the urgent need to address pressing environmental, social, economic, and academic challenges in an increasingly interconnected world. Universities, as hubs of knowledge creation, innovation, and societal influence, are uniquely positioned to lead the transition toward sustainable practices, serving as role models for communities and industries. The concept of sustainability in HEIs extends beyond envi ronmental stewardship to encompass social equity, economic viability, and academic excellence, aligning with global frameworks such as the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). However, achieving sustainability requires comprehensive tools to evaluate performance across these dimensions, ensuring alignment with the expectations of diverse stakeholders. The stakeholder theory, as articulated by Freeman (1984), emphasizes that organizations, including universities, must consider the needs and priorities of all relevant parties to achieve sustainable outcomes. In the context of HEIs, stakeholders are broadly categorized into internal and external groups. Internal stakeholders include students, who seek quality education and employability; faculty and researchers, who prioritize research opportunities and societal impact; administrative staff, who value suppo rtive work environments; and governance/leadership, who focus on strategic vision and resource allocation. External stakeholders encompass alumni, who contribute to institutional reputation; employers and industrial partners, who d

f, who value suppo rtive work environments; and governance/leadership, who focus on strategic vision and resource allocation. External stakeholders encompass alumni, who contribute to institutional reputation; employers and industrial partners, who demand skilled graduates a nd collaborative innovation; local communities and civil society, who expect social and environmental contributions; public authorities and regulators, who enforce compliance and policy alignment; funders and donors, who seek measurable impact; and prospective students and parents, who prioritize educational quality and career prospects. According to Mainardes et al. (2013), effective stakeholder management in HEIs requires integrating these diverse perspectives to foster trust, collaboration, and institutional legitimacy. 275/278

Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 4 The complexity of sustainability in HEIs necessitates robust, multidimensional evaluation tools that go beyond traditional metrics like academic rankings or financial performance. Al. Pop et al. (2020) highlight the need for indices that incorporate environmental (e.g., carbon footprint, resource efficiency), social (e.g., diversity, community engagement), economic (e.g., financial sustainability, employability), and academic (e.g., research impact, teaching quality) dimensions. Existing frameworks provide valuable benchmarks but often lack comprehensive stakeholder input or methodological flexibility to capture context -specific priorities. The University Sustainability Performance Index (USPI) addresses this gap by leveraging the Multi-Attribute Utility Theory (MAUT) (Keeney and Raiffa, 1993) to systematically aggregate stakeholder preferences into a synthetic index. MAUT’s strength lies in its ability to handle multiple criteria and stakeholder priorities, offering a scientifically rigorous yet ada ptable framework for assessing university sustainability. The development of the USPI responds to the growing demand for transparent, stakeholder - driven tools that enable universities to assess their performance, identify areas for improvement, and align with global sustainability goals. By engaging both internal and external stakeholders, the USPI aims to foster a holistic approach to sustainability, ensuring that universities not only meet regulatory and societal expectations but also drive innovation and leadership in sustainable development. This project will produce six high -impact scientific articles, each exploring specific stakeholder perspectives or the overarching methodology, contributing to the academic fields of sustainability, stakeholder theory, and multi -criteria decision analysis while providing pr actical tools for university leaders, policymakers, and stakeholders worldwide. Main Objective The primary objective is to design and develop the University Sustainability Performance Index (USPI), a comprehensive synthetic index to assess the sustainability performance of universities by aggregating the preferences of internal and external stakeholders using the Multi-Attribute Utility Theory ( MAUT) (Keeney and Raiffa, 1993). The project aims to produce eight scientific articles for publication in high -impact journals, contributing to advancements in university sustainability, stakeholder management, and multi-criteria decision analysis. Specific Objectives 1. Map the research landscape on university sustainability through bibliometric analysis. 2. Extract insights from academic papers using text mining to identify key themes and gaps. 3. Analyze sustainability preferences of students and faculty. 4. Examine governance and administrative perspectives on sustainability performance. 5. Investigate external stakeholders’ expectations (alumni, employers, prospective students/parents). 6. Integrate public, civic, and financial stakeholders’ perspectives into the sustainability index. 7. Design a MAUT-based composite index and apply it to pilot universities. 276/278

Methodology General Approach The USPI project adopts a multidisciplinary approach to develop a comprehensive, stakeholder-driven index for assessing university sustainability performance across environmental, social, economic, and academic dimensions. This approach integrates four complementary research methodologies —bibliometric analysis , text mining , empirical methods, and decision-making methods —to ensure a robust, scientifically rigorous framework that captures both the academic landscape and stakeholder perspectives. At the core of this integration lies the Multi-Attribute Utility Theory (MAUT) (Keeney and Raiffa, 1993), which serves as the primary framework for synthesizing stakeholder preferences into a single, cohesive index. • Bibliometric Analysis: Maps the academic landscape of university sustainability and stakeholder engagement, identifying key trends, influential works, and research gaps using tools like VOSviewer and Bibliometrix (or by using Python) . This provides a quantitative overview of the field, informing MAUT criteria selection. • Text Mining: Complements bibliometric analysis by extracting thematic insights from academic literature using natural language processing (NLP) techniques (e.g., topic modeling, sentiment analysis), identifying nuanced concepts and stakeholder references to refine MAUT criteria. • Empirical Methods : Capture stakeholder preferences through mixed -methods (surveys, focus groups) and qualitative approaches (interviews, case studies), ensuring the USPI reflects real-world priorities and informs MAUT weightings. • Decision-Making Methods: Utilize MAUT to synthesize bibliometric, text-mined, and empirical data into a composite index, with criteria defined

(interviews, case studies), ensuring the USPI reflects real-world priorities and informs MAUT weightings. • Decision-Making Methods: Utilize MAUT to synthesize bibliometric, text-mined, and empirical data into a composite index, with criteria defined, weights assigned via AHP/Delphi, and robustness tested through sensitivity analysis. • Integration: Teams collaborate through data-sharing protocols (e.g., shared databases, workshops) to ensure findings from each method inform the others. For example, text mining may highlight digital sustainability, prompting stakeholder surveys to include it, with MAUT integrating all inputs into the USPI. This approach ensures the USPI is theoretically grounded, stakeholder -driven, and practically relevant, producing seven high-impact articles and a usable sustainability index. Livrable 2 – Production Pédagogique A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 1.1.1 Écosystème LMS et plateformes pédagogiques. L’environnement numérique d’apprentissage d’ESB s’appuie sur quatre plateformes complémen- taires :Moodle, Blackboard, Tekouinet ESB Platform. Moodle a été mobilisée pour la continuité pédagogique, la gestion des ressources, les examens en ligne et l’accompagnement des enseignants, notamment durant la période COVID. Depuis2023, ESB a engagé une migration progressive versBlackboard, nouvel environnement institutionnel de scénarisation pédagogique, structuré autour de parcours d’apprentissage, de séquencesAvant / Pendant / Aprèset de dispositifs d’Adaptive Learning. Tekouin, dont j’assure l’administration depuis2020, est dédiée aux enseignements quantitatifs, à la programmation et à l’évaluation en ligne. Elle a permis d’accompagner4959 étudiants, avec 19733 occurrences d’usage cumuléeset jusqu’à56 groupessimultanés. Enfin,ESB Platformest un projet personnel développé dans le cadre de mes travaux RDI avec AI4U. Cette plateforme vise à renforcer la digitalisation du suivi pédagogique, de l’encadrement et de l’accompagnement académique des étudiants. Le projet est actuellement en phase de finalisation, avec une première phase de test prévue au mois de juin. Pour le détail relatif à Tekouin — intérêt pédagogique, évolution 2020–2025 et rôle d’adminis- tration — voir Section 3,Intégration de technologies, Focus Tekouin. Table 1. The PLAR (Program Learning Assessment Review) is the programme-level quality auditrequired by BGA. It aggregates the CARs of the constituent courses (§ 4) along the Introduced/Reinforced/ Emphasized (I/R/E) trajectory in order to evaluate thedegree of attainment of each Program Learning Outcome (PLO)and to drive continuous improvement at programme level. Methodology – 5-section PLAR template Reporting structure (one document per PLO trajectory).Each PLAR follows a five-section template, harmonised across the three IMA programmes audited (BA, LBC-BI, LBC-BIS) : 1. Section 1 – Program Learning Outcomes– table of the programme’s PLOs, withCom- mon/Specifictyping (Common PLOs are SDG-aligned and shared across IMA programmes; Specific PLOs are unique to the programme). 2. Section 2 – Methodology– selection of the PLOs to assess (typically≥2 per programme : one Common, SDG-alignedand oneSpecific), and selection of the contributing courses along the I/R/E trajectory. 3. Section 3 – Benchmark Indicator (MBI)– theMinimum Benchmark Indicatoris set at 60% : a PLO is considered achieved when the percentage of students scoring≥60% on the related CLOs reaches the threshold. 4. Section 4 – Results– per-CLO performance, per-course consolidation, per-PLO aggregation, and overall verdict (goal met / not met). 5. Section 5 – Recommendations for Continuous Improvement– corrective actions feeding back into syllabi, course scheduling, assessment design and faculty training. Selection rule (CLOs→PLOs). For each course mapped to a selected PLO, the CLOs already linked to the PLO via the alignment matr

uous Improvement– corrective actions feeding back into syllabi, course scheduling, assessment design and faculty training. Selection rule (CLOs→PLOs). For each course mapped to a selected PLO, the CLOs already linked to the PLO via the alignment matrix (§ 2) are extracted, and the percentage of students reaching the 60% benchmark on each of these CLOs is computed. ThePLO attainment ratefor the course is the mean of its PLO-related CLOs; theprogramme-level PLO attainmentis the mean across courses along the I/R/E trajectory. Indicators computed for each PLAR. — Attainment rate per PLO(% of students reaching the 60% benchmark, aggregated across the I/R/E trajectory). — Pedagogical coverage of each PLO(number of contributing courses, distribution across I/R/E levels and semesters). — CLO-to-PLO traceability(per-CLO performance feeding back into the PLO score). — CAR→PLAR consistency (alignment between module-level CAR observations and programme-level PLO profile). — Action planfor the next cohort (curriculum revision, course scheduling, assessment design, faculty training). Tooling and frequency. — Data sources: CAR results (§ 4), CLO→PLO alignment matrix (§ 2), grade extracts from Tekouin/ESB IS. — Consolidation : master spreadsheetPLOs Assessment (IMA).ods (one row per course, one column per CLO, weighted aggregation per PLO). 23/49 195/227

Deux briques scientifiques actuellementen cours de révisionstructurent cet axe : (i) l’Orchestrated N-Agent Centipede Game Framework for Cooperative Artificial Intelligence Systems(Ben Brik, auteur unique) qui étend le jeu classique de Rosenthal (1981) àN agents pilotés par un orchestrateur central, fournissant un benchmark game-théorique de la coopération sous tension bénéfice individuel court-termevs performance collective long-terme; (ii) le cadre Mean Field Reinforcement Learning for LLM-Based Pedagogical Agents in Higher Education (proposal doctoral) qui modélise la cohorte étudiante comme une distribution de population mt(x) = 1 N ∑ iδxi(t) et une politique πθ(at |xi(t),mt) conditionnée à la fois sur l’état individuel et sur l’étatcollectif, dans la lignée des Mean Field Games deLasry & Lions (2007). Le projet adresse les limitations des applications existantes en automatisant le suivi alimentaire via des modèles CNN (VGG16 et MobileNetV2) et en générant des plans nutritionnels adaptatifs grâce à un système RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) avec Llama 3.1. L'architecture microservices, développée avec React.js, Node.js/Express et Python/FastAPI, permet une intégration fluide des composants IA. La méthodologie hybride allie CRISP-DM pour le développement des modèles IA et Scrum pour le cycle de développement logiciel. Les résultats démontrent une précision de 87% en reconnaissance visuelle, une amélioration de 40% sur les objectifs protéiques, et une réduction de 70% du temps de saisie utilisateur. SmartNutriTrack représente une avancée significative dans les applications de nutrition digitale, offrant une solution complète et scientifiquement fondée pour le suivi et la planification nutritionnelle personnalisée. ign and development of SmartNutriTrack, an innovative intelligent nutrition application that combines computer vision-based food recognition and personalized meal planning. The project addresses limitations of existing applications by automating food tracking through CNN models (VGG16 and MobileNetV2) and generating adaptive nutrition plans using a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system with Llama 3.1. The microservices architecture, developed with React.js, Node.js/Express and Python/FastAPI, enables seamless integration of AI components. The hybrid methodology combines CRISP-DM for AI model development and Scrum for the software development cycle. Results demonstrate 87% accuracy in visual recognition, 40% improvement in protein targets achievement, and 70% reduction in user input time. SmartNutriTrack represents a significant advancement in digital nutrition applications, providing a comprehensive and scientifically-grounded solution for personalized nutrition tracking and planning. Livrable 3 – Rapport de Synthèse A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 Annexe E – SDAI’24 et SDAI’25 : programmes officiels Contexte. La journée scientifique internationaleSDAI (Scientific Discovery in the Light of Artificial Intelligence) est l’événement annuel phare de l’unité de rechercheAI4U (Esprit Tech) basée à l’Esprit School of Business. Elle rassemble des chercheurs et praticiens internationaux autour des applications de l’IA, et constitue une vitrine de la production scientifique d’AI4U auprès de la communauté académique et industrielle. Édition SDAI’24(03/05/2024, ESB) – thème général :IA appliquée. 9 intervenants internatio- naux (Canada, Danemark, France, Arabie Saoudite, USA, Tunisie) ont présenté des travaux en assurance, santé, urbanisme, finance et représentation par graphes.Rôle d’Aymen Ben Brik : membre du comité organisateur (équipe de 11 membres avec H. Abidi, A. Baghdadi, R. Ammar, I. Rebhi, S. Souli, S. Besbes, I. Ben Fredj, S. Benzarti, S. Belhaj Rhouma)et modérateur de la journée. Édition SDAI’25(17/10/2025, ESB) – thème spécifique :Cybersécurité augmentée par l’IA. 8 intervenants (dont Imed Zitouni, ex-Google) ont couvert la détection de menaces pilotée par l’IA, la conformité ISO 27001, le cadre réglementaire tunisien et la révolution LLM.Rôle d’Aymen Ben Brik : Head of AI4U Research Unit(responsable scientifique de l’événement) et membre du comité organisateur (équipe de 24 membres). Programmes officiels intégraux. Les deux programmes imprimés sont reproduits ci- après (couverture + composition du comité organisateur + programme détaillé des sessions). Slim Bechikh, University of Carthage, Tunisia Biography Slim Bechikh, PhD and Habilitation degrees in Business Informatics from the University of Tunis, ISG-Tunis, Tunisia, is currently Full Professor with the University of Carthage, FSEG-Nabeul, Tunisia. He is also a Research Director within the SMART laboratory, ISG-Tunis, University of Tunis, Tunisia. He published over 100 papers in peer-reviewed journals and refereed conferences. His current research interests include evolutionary optimization, machine learning, deep neural networks, business analytics, and SBSE. Dr. Bechikh was a recipient of the Best Paper Award of the ACM SAC-2010 in Switzerland. He supervised the Tunisian best national Doctoral thesis in ICT for the year 2019, which earned a presidential prize in scientific research and technology. He was promoted to the grade of IEEE Senior Member by August 2021. He is Associate Editor for IEEE Transactions on Evolutionay Computation and Swarm and evolutionary Computation. He serves as reviewer for over 80 international journals in AI and its applications. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 From Intelligent Tutoring Systems to Shared Cognition: Rethinking Collaborative Learning in the University of the Future Executive Summary Background and Problem Relevance: Large language Models (LLMs) are rapidly shaping the landscape of Higher Education (HE) by providing students with on-demand feedback, explanations, answers to assigned tasks, and writing assistance. However , most current applications of LLMs remain individualized whereby students use them privately. This current trend reinforces individualized cognition, overlooks the social dimension of learning, and hinders opportunities for peer collaboration, dialogue, shared reasoning, and co - construction of knowledge which are key pillars of Project Based Learning (PBL). In fact, among the critical criticism of LLMs in HE is their tendency to atomize learning communities, replacing group interactions and dialogue with individualized consultations. From a strategic perspective, ESPRIT’s historical leadership in PBL has conferred a first-mover advantage that is increasingly eroded through institutional imitation. This proposal posits that the next frontier of ESPRIT pedagogical innovation lies not in further individual augmentation, but in the orchestration of shared cognition between humans and AI . Accordingly, this research adopts an exploratory and design-oriented perspective to reposition ESPRIT as a model for the University of the Future. It seeks to reconceptualize LLMs not as private tutors, but as collaborative cognitive partners embedded within group learning processes. In essence, this proposal seeks (1) to explore how ESPRIT can transform the use of LLMs from private tutors into collaborative cognitive partners to support team -bas

, but as collaborative cognitive partners embedded within group learning processes. In essence, this proposal seeks (1) to explore how ESPRIT can transform the use of LLMs from private tutors into collaborative cognitive partners to support team -based projects ethically and responsibly and (2) to design, implement, and evaluate a prototype platform for human-AI shared cognition and collaborative learning through the use of multi -agent systems for brainstorming and moderation to ensure equitable contribution, reflections, consensus - building, and knowledge synthesis. Research aims and objectives : This proposal aims to investigate how LLMs can be designed and used to support shared cognition and collaborative learning , rather than simple individualized problem solving. Its primary objectives are to: - Empirically analyze current patterns of LLM usage among ESPRIT students and their implications for collaborative practices. - Identify key cognitive, social, and technological design principles that foster effective AI- mediated collaboration, including shared metacognition, equitable participation, and consensus-building. - Design, implement, and evaluate an AI -mediated multi -agent collaborative learning platform (AI-CLP) explicitly optimized for group-based learning contexts. 143/419

Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 - Develop a theoretically grounded and practice-oriented framework to guide faculty in the ethical and responsible integration of AI within PBL environments. Research Methodology: This research is anchored in an integrative theoretical framework drawing on Social Constructivism (Vygotsky, 1978), Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning – CSCL (Silverman, 1995) ) and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge – TPACK Framework (Mishra and Koehler, 2006) . We plan to adopt a Design Research (DR) approach to iteratively design, build and validate our proposed collaborative AI learning platform. The research is structured into four interconnected phases: Phase 1 – Literature review and exploratory study : We will first expand the current literature review performed by the core team to synthesize the state of the art in AI-mediated collaborative learning approaches and platforms and further refine our research contribution. We will propose a theoretical framework that will guide the development of our proposed platform. We will then conduct surveys among ESPRIT students on their current LLM use, collaboration challenges and perception of AI as a potential social collaborative partner in group projects. Phase 2 – System Analysis, Design and Implementation: We will start by articulating the functional and non -functional requirements of the AI -mediated collaborative learning platform (AI-CLP). Special focus will be devoted to wards the i ntegration of ethics and Responsible AI principles (fairness, transparency, explainability, privacy, and human oversight) by design. Using a modular platform, we will then iteratively implement AI-CLP using open-source LLMs as multi-agent systems while adhering to a user-cen

Responsible AI principles (fairness, transparency, explainability, privacy, and human oversight) by design. Using a modular platform, we will then iteratively implement AI-CLP using open-source LLMs as multi-agent systems while adhering to a user-centric approach based on evolutionary prototype, while maintaining human agency and oversight. Phase 3 – Pilot Study: We will conduct a controlled exploratory empirical study involving 100 students from ESE and ESB to assess the merit of AI-CLP . We will consider two groups of students : control (Individual-AI) groups where students use AI privately and Shared-AI groups where students interact with multi- agent facilitators to complete a common team - based project. Chat Logs, direct observations, reflection notes and surveys will be used for comparative purposes. The outcomes will be used to further refine AI-CLP in future iterations. Phase 4 – Research Dissemination : We will produce a final report to document our research findings and present concrete recommendations to ESPRIT senior management team on how to leverage AI-CLP to renew its positi oning as a leader in pedagogical innovation. Seminars and workshops will be conducted to disseminate the practical implications of our research among fellow faculty , admins, and students. We also plan to disseminate our research results through academic conferences and peer-reviewed journal publications. 144/419

Livrable 3 – Rapport de Synthèse A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 3 Technical Note: University Sustainability Performance Index (USPI) Project 1. Context and Objectives Context Sustainability in higher education institutions (HEIs) has emerged as a critical global priority, driven by the urgent need to address pressing environmental, social, economic, and academic challenges in an increasingly interconnected world. Universities, as hubs of knowledge creation, innovation, and societal influence, are uniquely positioned to lead the transition toward sustainable practices, serving as role models for communities and industries. The concept of sustainability in HEIs extends beyond envi ronmental stewardship to encompass social equity, economic viability, and academic excellence, aligning with global frameworks such as the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). However, achieving sustainability requires comprehensive tools to evaluate performance across these dimensions, ensuring alignment with the expectations of diverse stakeholders. The stakeholder theory, as articulated by Freeman (1984), emphasizes that organizations, including universities, must consider the needs and priorities of all relevant parties to achieve sustainable outcomes. In the context of HEIs, stakeholders are broadly categorized into internal and external groups. Internal stakeholders include students, who seek quality education and employability; faculty and researchers, who prioritize research opportunities and societal impact; administrative staff, who value suppo rtive work environments; and governance/leadership, who focus on strategic vision and resource allocation. External stakeholders encompass alumni, who contribute to institutional reputation; employers and industrial partners,

staff, who value suppo rtive work environments; and governance/leadership, who focus on strategic vision and resource allocation. External stakeholders encompass alumni, who contribute to institutional reputation; employers and industrial partners, who demand skilled graduates a nd collaborative innovation; local communities and civil society, who expect social and environmental contributions; public authorities and regulators, who enforce compliance and policy alignment; funders and donors, who seek measurable impact; and prospective students and parents, who prioritize educational quality and career prospects. According to Mainardes et al. (2013), effective stakeholder management in HEIs requires integrating these diverse perspectives to foster trust, collaboration, and institutional legitimacy. 150/419

Livrable 3 – Rapport de Synthèse A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 4 The complexity of sustainability in HEIs necessitates robust, multidimensional evaluation tools that go beyond traditional metrics like academic rankings or financial performance. Al. Pop et al. (2020) highlight the need for indices that incorporate environmental (e.g., carbon footprint, resource efficiency), social (e.g., diversity, community engagement), economic (e.g., financial sustainability, employability), and academic (e.g., research impact, teaching quality) dimensions. Existing frameworks provide valuable benchmarks but often lack comprehensive stakeholder input or methodological flexibility to capture context -specific priorities. The University Sustainability Performance Index (USPI) addresses this gap by leveraging the Multi-Attribute Utility Theory (MAUT) (Keeney and Raiffa, 1993) to systematically aggregate stakeholder preferences into a synthetic index. MAUT’s strength lies in its ability to handle multiple criteria and stakeholder priorities, offering a scientifically rigorous yet ada ptable framework for assessing university sustainability. The development of the USPI responds to the growing demand for transparent, stakeholder - driven tools that enable universities to assess their performance, identify areas for improvement, and align with global sustainability goals. By engaging both internal and external stakeholders, the USPI aims to foster a holistic approach to sustainability, ensuring that universities not only meet regulatory and societal expectations but also drive innovation and leadership in sustainable development. Main Objective The primary objective is to design and develop the University Sustainability Performance Index (USPI), a comprehensive synthetic index to assess the sustainability performance of universities by aggregating the preferences of internal and external stakeholders using the Multi-Attribute Utility Theory ( MAUT) (Keeney and Raiffa, 1993). The project aims to produce eight scientific articles for publication in high -impact journals, contributing to advancements in university sustainability, stakeholder management, and multi-criteria decision analysis. Specific Objectives 1. Map the research landscape on university sustainability through bibliometric analysis. 2. Extract insights from academic papers using text mining to identify key themes and gaps. 3. Analyze sustainability preferences of students and faculty. 4. Examine governance and administrative perspectives on sustainability performance. 5. Investigate external stakeholders’ expectations (alumni, employers, prospective students/parents). 6. Methodology General Approach The USPI project adopts a multidisciplinary approach to develop a comprehensive, stakeholder-driven index for assessing university sustainability performance across environmental, social, economic, and academic dimensions. This approach integrates four complementary research methodologies —bibliometric analysis , text mining , empirical methods, and decision-making methods —to ensure a robust, scientifically rigorous framework that captures both the academic landscape and stakeholder perspectives. At the core of this integration lies the Multi-Attribute Utility Theory (MAUT) (Keeney and Raiffa, 1993), which serves as the primary framework for synthesizing stakeholder preferences into a single, cohesive index. • Bibliometric Analysis: Maps the academic landscape of university sustainability and stakeholder engagement, identifying key trends, influential works, and research gaps using tools like VOSviewer and Bibliometrix (or by using Python) . This provides a quantitative overview of the field, informing MAUT criteria selection. • Text Mining: Complements bibliometric analysis by extracting thematic insights from academic literature using natural language processing (NLP) techniques (e.g., topic modeling, sentiment analysis), identifying nuanced concepts and stakeholder references to refine MAUT criteria. • Empirical Methods : Capture stakeholder preferences through mixed -methods (surveys, focus groups) and qualitative approaches (interviews, case studies), ensuring the USPI reflects real-world priorities and informs MAUT weightings. • Decision-Making Methods: Utilize MAUT to synthesize bibliometric, text-mined, and empirical data into a composite index, with criteria de

ches (interviews, case studies), ensuring the USPI reflects real-world priorities and informs MAUT weightings. • Decision-Making Methods: Utilize MAUT to synthesize bibliometric, text-mined, and empirical data into a composite index, with criteria defined, weights assigned via AHP/Delphi, and robustness tested through sensitivity analysis. • Integration: Teams collaborate through data-sharing protocols (e.g., shared databases, workshops) to ensure findings from each method inform the others. For example, text mining may highlight digital sustainability, prompting stakeholder surveys to include it, with MAUT integrating all inputs into the USPI. This approach ensures the USPI is theoretically grounded, stakeholder -driven, and practically relevant, producing seven high-impact articles and a usable sustainability index.
