Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 Résumés Samir BEN HARIZ (Enseignant-Chercheur, LMM-IRA, Le Mans Université) Titre : Changements structurels : méthodes de détection et applications Résumé : La stabilité des modèles est une condition fondamentale en modélisation, que ce soit en finance, en assurance ou encore en climatologie. Dans cet exposé, nous présenterons différentes techniques de détection des ruptures dans les modèles statistiques. Nous aborderons également plusieurs exemples d’applications potentielles sur des données financières et environnementales. Wissal SABBAGH (Enseignante-Chercheuse, LMM-IRA, Le Mans Université) Titre : Gestion du risque cyber avec contrôle impulsionnel Résumé : La cybercriminalité constitue une menace critique pour les institutions publiques comme pour les organisations privées, fragilisant ainsi la résilience du paysage financier et économique mondial. Les pertes mondiales dues à la cybercriminalité sont estimées à 1 % du PIB, soit environ mille milliards de dollars chaque année. Comme l’a souligné Jerome Powell, président de la Réserve fédérale américaine, les cyberattaques représentent aujourd’hui le risque le plus important pour le système financier. Dans cette présentation, nous introduisons une étude de référence dans laquelle le propriétaire d’un cluster cherche à sécuriser un réseau informatique contre des cyberattaques en effectuant régulièrement des mises à jour ou en acquérant des solutions de s écurité. L’absence de protection adéquate peut entraîner d’importantes pertes financières, tandis qu’une intrusion réussie peut infecter le réseau et provoquer des incidents majeurs pour le propriétaire du cluster et ses clients. Nous commençons par caractériser la politique de protection optimale dans

er d’importantes pertes financières, tandis qu’une intrusion réussie peut infecter le réseau et provoquer des incidents majeurs pour le propriétaire du cluster et ses clients. Nous commençons par caractériser la politique de protection optimale dans un scénario de piratage. En nous appuyant sur un modèle épidémiologique, nous mettons en évidence une stratégie de défense dynamique qui s’adapte à l’évolution des méthodes d’attaque et au degré d’infection du réseau. Nous abordons ensuite les défis d’optimisation via des approches d’apprentissage profond, en recourant à ces méthodes pour approximer les solutions d’un système d’équations entièrement couplées. Il s’agit d’un travail réalisé en collaboration avec C. Hillairet (ENSAE-CREST, IP Paris) et T. Mastrolia (Berkeley University, USA). Wajd MESKINI (Senior data Scientist chez omni:us) Titre : Impact de l'IA Act sur l'assurance et IA de confiance" Résumé : L'usage grandissant de l'IA en assurance représente une opportunité pour le secteur, mais aussi un risque réglementaire - entre autres. Cet exposé décrit l'impact de la dernière réglementation européenne sur l'IA sur le secteur de l'assurance et ses différents usages possibles, et un segment sur l'interprétation de modèles en boîte noire et sa contribution à établir une IA de confiance 190/419

Livrable 3 – Rapport de Synthèse A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 Wiem SABBAGH (Chargée d’Etudes Actuarielles chez AXA XL) Titre : Du Conflit à la Couverture: Modéliser et Maîtriser le Risque GEMP Grèves, Émeutes et Mouvements Populaires Résumé : Dans ce travail on s’intéresse dans un premier temps à la définition du risque GEMP (grèves, émeutes et mouvements populaires) tout en mettant en évidence, à travers l’analyse historique de ces événements, leur impact financier significatif sur les secteurs de l'assurance et de la réassurance. On présente par la suite les méth odes statistiques et probabilistes employées pour modéliser efficacement ces risques dans le domaine assurantiel. Youssef ESSTAFA (Enseignant-Chercheur, LMM-IRA, Le Mans Université) Titre : Gradient boosting infinitésimal Résumé : Nous étudions le comportement asymptotique des algorithmes de gradient boosting lorsque le taux d'apprentissage tend vers zéro et que le nombre d'itérations est ajusté en conséquence. Nous considérons principalement le L2-boosting pour la régression avec un apprenant de base linéaire, tel qu'étudié dans Bühlmann et Yu (2003). Nous prouvons l'existence d'une limite déterministe et la caractérisons comme la solution unique d'une équation différentielle linéaire dans un espace de fonctions de dimension infinie. Ces algorithmes ont montré leur efficacité dans divers domaines, et en particulier en actuariat, où ils permettent d'améliorer la précision des modèles de prévision tout en optimisant les calculs, ce qui est crucial pour des analyses plus rapides et plus fiables. Amel Hedhli (Enseignante-Chercheuse, Esprit) Titre : Modélisation du Risque financier : Étude Comparative entre l’Approche GJR -GARCH couplée aux Vine Copulas et les Modèles du deep learning Résumé : La modélisatio

lyses plus rapides et plus fiables. Amel Hedhli (Enseignante-Chercheuse, Esprit) Titre : Modélisation du Risque financier : Étude Comparative entre l’Approche GJR -GARCH couplée aux Vine Copulas et les Modèles du deep learning Résumé : La modélisation de la Value-at-Risk (VaR) constitue un outil essentiel pour les investisseurs financiers, en leur offrant un cadre quantitatif pour évaluer le risque de perte potentielle de leurs portefeuilles et optimiser leurs décisions de gestion du capital. La présente étud e propose une comparaison entre deux grandes catégories de méthodes d’évaluation du risque : d’une part, les approches statistiques classiques, notamment le modèle GJR -GARCH associé aux copules en vigne (Vine Copulas), et d’autre part, les techniques d’app rentissage automatique. Elle poursuit un double objectif : premièrement, pallier les limites des approches standards de la VaR, notamment dans des contextes marqués par des événements extrêmes, en introduisant une méthode empirique alternative ; deuxièmement, contribuer à la littérature en abordant spécifiquement la problématique de la mesure du risque dans la région MENA (Moyen -Orient et Afrique du Nord), encore peu explorée dans ce domaine. 191/419

Cette évolution soulève de nouveaux enjeux pour l’actuariat, notamment en ce qui concerne la disponibilité des données sur ces véhicules encore peu représentés dans les portefeuilles, le risque de biais dans les modèles prédictifs, ainsi que la nécessité d ’adapter les approches tarifaires et les critères de sous cription à ces profils de risque émergents. HONORIS AI Academic Task Force Concept Note December 13, 2024 Subject: Appointment to the Honoris AI Academic Task Force and Assigned Missions Dear Members, As part of Honoris’ strategic priorities to enhance the quality and relevance of our educational offerings, I am pleased to confirm your appointment to the Academic Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (AI). This Task Force, organized by key disciplinary “Verticals” and composed of representatives from all our partner institutions, is mandated to fully explore and leverage the potential of AI across all academic activities. • Context and Vision: The growing adoption of AI technologies in higher education drives us to rethink our pedagogical approaches to better equip students for an increasingly digital world. Our goal is to improve the quality of learning, boost graduate employability, and foster innovation throughout Honoris institutions. • Mission of the Task Force: 1. Recommend tools, methodologies, and resources to support the design, implementation, and evaluation of AI-enhanced learning environments. 2. Propose internal policies to support the sustainable integration of AI solutions, focusing on maintaining quality and long-term effectiveness. 3. Embark on Curricular Reform initiatives by integrating AI into our teaching and content development methods, allowing us to create dynamic, adaptive, and personalized learning experiences for students. 4. Develop institutional guidelines for the ethical and responsible use of AI in teaching, research, academic administration and among students. Include standards to ensure data protection and privacy. 5. Strengthen inter-institutional cooperation to share best practice

Livrable 3 – Rapport de Synthèse A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 International Journal of Quality and Service Sciences What Makes a University Sustainable in the Eyes of its Core Community? Sustainability Expectation–Perception Gap Purpose –This study adopts a behavioural, stakeholder centred approach to identify the key dimensions of university sustainability valued by internal stakeholders (students, faculty members and administrative staff). It examines how they prioritize environmental, social, and economic dimensions, assesses gaps between expectations and perceived initiatives, and proposes a composite score to support the University Sustainability Performance Index (USPI). Design/methodology/approach – This study uses a qualitative case study approach within a single university, conducting semi -structured interviews with internal stakeholders to explore perceptions of environmental, social, and economic sustainability. Thematic analysis identified sustainability university dimensions. Findings – The results reveal gaps between stakeholder perceptions and expectations. Socially, student well -being and community engag ement need stronger structuring. Environmental initiatives are recognized, yet sustainable mobility and awareness require better formalization. Economic gaps remain significant, especially in energy optimization, financial governance and sustainable investment. Research limitations – The study focuses on internal stakeholders in a specific context. Future research could include external stakeholders and cross-institutional comparisons. Practical implications – The USPI provides university leaders with a transparent, stakeholder- driven decision-support tool to assess sustainability performance and prioritize strategic actions effectively. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 International Journal of Quality and Service Sciences Introduction Sustainability in higher education institutions (HEIs) has become a strategic and societal imperative in response to growing environmental, social, economic, and governance challenges worldwide (Velazquez et al., 2006; Alshuwaikhat & Abubakar, 2008). Universities are no longer perceived solely as knowledge-producing entities; they are increasingly expected to act as transformative agents capable of shaping sustainable development trajectories (Popowska & Sady, 2024; Sugiarto et al., 2022). In alignment with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), sustainability in HEIs extends beyond environmental stewardship to encompass social equity, economic viability, institutional governance, and academic excellence (Alshuwaikhat et al., 2016). Despite the proliferation of sustainability rankings, reporting frameworks, and performance indicators, existing assessment tools often remain predominantly operational and managerial in nature (Sonetti et al., 2016; Horan & O’Regan, 2021). They typically rely on externally defined metrics and institutional reporting mechanisms, while giving limited attention to how sustainability is perceived and pri oritized by the university’s own academic community. This represents a significant conceptual gap. Sustainability is not merely a technical or administrative construct; it is also a socially constructed and behaviourally interpreted phenomenon shaped by stakeholder perceptions, expectations, and value systems (Dagiliūtė et al., 2018; Zhao & Zou, 2023). Stakeholder theory (Freeman, 1984) posits that organizational sustainability depends on the integration of diverse stakeholder interests. Within

by stakeholder perceptions, expectations, and value systems (Dagiliūtė et al., 2018; Zhao & Zou, 2023). Stakeholder theory (Freeman, 1984) posits that organizational sustainability depends on the integration of diverse stakeholder interests. Within HEIs, intern al stakeholders, particularly students and faculty, play a central role in shaping the institution’s sustainability identity (Alshuwaikhat & Abubakar, 2008; Disterheft et al., 2013). Students seek meaningful education, employability, and ethical alignment with societal challenges, while faculty members emphasize academic integrity, research impact, and institutional mission. Yet, little empirical research has systematically examined how these core actors interpret sustainability, how they prioritize its dim ensions, and how they evaluate institutional performance relative to their expectations (Dagiliūtė et al., 2018; Yasin et al., 2024). Addressing this gap is essential for developing assessment tools that genuinely reflect institutional realities rather than externally imposed benchmarks. If sustainability indices are to guide strategic decision -making effectively, they must be grounded in stakeholder -defined priorities (Velazquez et al., 2006; Alshuwaikhat et al., 2016). In this context, understanding what makes a university “sustainable” in the eyes of its core community becomes a critical research question. This study adopts a behavioural and stakeholder centred perspective to analyse the sustainability preferences of students, faculty members, and administrative staff within a case- study university. Through qualitative inquiry, it explores how these actors interpret environmental, social, and economic sustainability dimensions, how they hierarchize them, and how they perceive institutional performance.

Ultimately, it seeks to provide both theoretical insight and practical guidance for developing more legitimate, inclusive, and socially resonant sustainability assessment frameworks. Literature review Stakeholder Theory and University Sustainability Stakeholder theory provides a foundational lens for understanding sustainability in higher education institutions (HEIs). Originally developed in strategic management (Freeman, 1984), the theory argues that organizational legitimacy and long -term performance depend on the ability to recognize, balance, and integrate the interests of multiple stakeholder groups rather than privileging a single dom inant constituency. Organizations are embedded in networks of relationships, and value is generated through ongoing interactions among actors with diverse expectations. Mitchell et al., (1997) introduced the stakeholder salience framework, emphasizing that stakeholders differ in terms of power, legitimacy, and urgency. Within HEIs, a wide range of stakeholders coexist, including students, faculty members, administrative staff, employers, accreditation bodies, local communities, and policymakers. However, in ternal stakeholders, particularly students and faculty, occupy a structurally central position. They are not only recipients of sustainability policies but active agents who interpret, enact, and sometimes contest institutional sustainability agendas. More recent developments in stakeholder theory emphasize relationalit

urally central position. They are not only recipients of sustainability policies but active agents who interpret, enact, and sometimes contest institutional sustainability agendas. More recent developments in stakeholder theory emphasize relationality and value co-creation (Freeman et al., 2010). From this perspective, sustainability is not merely implemented through top-down governance mechanisms or infrastructure investments; it emerge s from shared meaning-making processes and collective engagement. Universities can thus be understood as ecosystems in which sustainability outcomes are co -produced through interactions between institutional strategies and stakeholder perceptions. While st akeholder theory provides a strong normative and relational foundation for understanding sustainability in higher education, the empirical literature on campus sustainability has developed along several thematic trajectories. Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) are increasingly recognized as pivotal actors in fostering sustainable development and addressing global environmental challenges. Often described as "small cities" due to their significant populations and complex operations (Alshuwaikhat & Abubakar, 2008; Velazquez et al., 2006; Min -Allah & Alrashed, 2020; Murshed, 2020), universities wield substantial direct and indirect impacts on the environment through their energy consumption, material use, waste generation, and daily activities. Consequently, the concept of a "green campus" has emerged as a comprehensive approach to integrating sustainability principles across physical infrastructure, academic curricula, research, and institutional governance (Disterheft et al., 2013; Sugiarto et al., 2022). Conceptualization, Frameworks, and Assessment Tools for Green Campuses A significant portion of the lit erature focuses on defining, conceptualizing, and assessing sustainability within HEIs. Early work proposed comprehensive managerial models for a "sustainable university" (Velazquez et al., 2006) and integrated approaches to campus sustainability (Alshuwai khat & Abubakar, 2008). The evolving nature of "campus sustainability" is often understood in a broad sense, encompassing physical, educational, and institutional dimensions (Disterheft et al., 2013). Researchers note a shift from simplistic "going green" trends to a more holistic, systemic understanding that integrates environmental, social, and economic dimensions (Alshuwaikhat et al., 2016; Sugiarto et al., 2022; Popowska & Sady, 2024). The development and application of assessment tools and ranking syst ems are central to measuring progress and benchmarking sustainability efforts. Prominent examples include the UI GreenMetric World University Rankings (Fatah & Waro, 2025) and the Sustainability Tracking, Assessment & Rating System (STARS) (Urbanski & Leal, 2015; Zhu & Dewancker, 2021; Washington-Ottombre, 2024). Other frameworks like AISHE (Auditing Instrument for Sustainability in Higher Education) (Lambrechts & Ceulemans, 2013) and SAQ (Sustainability Assessment Questionnaire) (Alshuwaikhat et al., 2016) are also utilized. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 International Journal of Quality and Service Sciences Governance, Policy, and Organizational Change Effective governance and strategic policy are crucial for embedding sustainability within HEIs. Strategic Planning & Institutionalization Papers emphasize the need for clear institutional frameworks (Alshuwaikhat et al., 2008) and strategic sustainability plans (Romero & Mulfarth, 2017). The integration of sustainability into institutional policies is seen as essential for long-term commitment (Da Silva et al., 2023). Barriers and Drivers to Implementation Research identifies various barriers, includi ng lack of awareness, knowledge, financial constraints, and resistance to change (Geh et al., 2024). Conversely, drivers include governmental pressure, financial savings, institutional leadership, and student interest (Geh et al., 2023). Organizational Learning & Reporting Sustainability r eporting is recognized as a tool for increasing organizational learning and strengthening sustainability efforts (Washington -Ottombre, 2024; Washington -Ottombre & Bigalke, 2018; Rosa et al., 2024). Smart Campus and Digitalization for Sustainability An emerging theme is the integration of smart technologies and digitalization to enhance campus sustainability. Smart Campus Concepts and Applications The " smart campus" concept leverages smart technologies with physical infrastructure for improved services, decision-making, and sustainability (Min-Allah & Alrashed, 2020; Sugiarto et al., 2022). This includes smart mi crogrids (Min -Allah & Alrashed, 2020), intelligent monitoring and visualization systems (Ceccarini et al., 2021), and IoT platforms for managing energy, water, and security (Subbarao et al., 2019). In this setting, we introduce a regulator whose objective is the reduction of cumulative emissions, in the spirit of Emission Trading Systems (ETS), where Ąrms must hold and trade permits to cover their emissions in a regulated market. The regulator acts as a central planner and controls the supply of permits, balancing emission reduction and aggregate output. Permits are allocated through a dynamic auction mechanism that adjusts supply in real time to achieve both market efficiency and the regulatorŠs long-term objectives. The regulator and the Ąrms interact through the endogenous permit price, which is determined by the regulatorŠs policy and affects ĄrmsŠ optimal strategies via the market clearing condition. The optimal regulator policy is derived within a Mean Field Control (MFC) framework. Exploiting the linear-quadratic structure and the presence of common noise, we characterise the equilibrium via a system of coupled FBSDEs and associated Riccati equation. Our results provide a tractable characterisation of optimal permit allocation policies in large economies and offer insights into the design of efficient emission trading mechanisms. Livrable 3 – Rapport de Synthèse A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 BGA Accreditation – ABB Activities A. Ben Brik | EFS-ELCCS 2026-2027 5. PLAR – Program Learning Assessment Review Definition. The PLAR (Program Learning Assessment Review) is the programme-level quality auditrequired by BGA. It aggregates the CARs of the constituent courses (§ 4) along the Introduced/Reinforced/ Emphasized (I/R/E) trajectory in order to evaluate thedegree of attainment of each Program Learning Outcome (PLO)and to drive continuous improvement at programme level. Methodology – 5-section PLAR template Reporting structure (one document per PLO trajectory).Each PLAR follows a five-section template, harmonised across the three IMA programmes audited (BA, LBC-BI, LBC-BIS) : 1. Section 1 – Program Learning Outcomes– table of the programme’s PLOs, withCom- mon/Specifictyping (Common PLOs are SDG-aligned and shared across IMA programmes; Specific PLOs are unique to the programme). 2. Section 2 – Methodology– selection of the PLOs to assess (typically≥2 per programme : one Common, SDG-alignedand oneSpecific), and selection of the contributing courses along the I/R/E trajectory. 3. Section 3 – Benchmark Indicator (MBI)– theMinimum Benchmark Indicatoris set at 60% : a PLO is considered achieved when the percentage of students scoring≥60% on the related CLOs reaches the threshold. 4. Section 4 – Results– per-CLO performance, per-course consolidation, per-PLO aggregation, and overall verdict (goal met / not met). 5. Section 5 – Recommendations for Continuous Improvement– corrective actions feeding back into syllabi, course scheduling, assessment design and faculty training. Selection rule (CLOs→PLOs). For each course mapped to a selected PLO, the CLOs already linked to the PLO via the alignment matrix

s Improvement– corrective actions feeding back into syllabi, course scheduling, assessment design and faculty training. Selection rule (CLOs→PLOs). For each course mapped to a selected PLO, the CLOs already linked to the PLO via the alignment matrix (§ 2) are extracted, and the percentage of students reaching the 60% benchmark on each of these CLOs is computed. ThePLO attainment ratefor the course is the mean of its PLO-related CLOs; theprogramme-level PLO attainmentis the mean across courses along the I/R/E trajectory. Indicators computed for each PLAR. — Attainment rate per PLO(% of students reaching the 60% benchmark, aggregated across the I/R/E trajectory). — Pedagogical coverage of each PLO(number of contributing courses, distribution across I/R/E levels and semesters). — CLO-to-PLO traceability(per-CLO performance feeding back into the PLO score). — CAR→PLAR consistency (alignment between module-level CAR observations and programme-level PLO profile). — Action planfor the next cohort (curriculum revision, course scheduling, assessment design, faculty training). Tooling and frequency. — Data sources: CAR results (§ 4), CLO→PLO alignment matrix (§ 2), grade extracts from Tekouin/ESB IS. — Consolidation : master spreadsheetPLOs Assessment (IMA).ods (one row per course, one column per CLO, weighted aggregation per PLO). 23/49 283/419

Contexte du projet et problématique (400 mots maximum) Dans Un contexte où l’éducation supérieure se digitalise rapidement, les établissements universitaires rencontrent plusieurs défis liés à la gestion des données étudiantes, à la qualité de l’enseignement et à l’efficacité des processus administratifs. Les méthode s traditionnelles, telles que la gestion papier des inscriptions, le suivi manuel des absences et la correction manuelle des examens, ne sont plus adaptées aux exigences d'une éducation moderne et aux attentes des étudiants et des enseignants. Le manque de solutions numériques intégrées rend la gestion des informations des étudiants inefficace et source d’erreurs. Par exemple, les inscriptions se font encore sur papier, ce qui est fastidieux et source de risques de perte ou de confusion des documents. De plus, le suivi des absences et de la participation en classe reste limité, rendant difficile l’identification des étudiants en difficulté ou ceux qui nécessitent un soutien supplémentaire.
